Toya Graham slapped her son, Michael, during a protest after seeing him with a brick, fearing he would get into trouble or follow in the footsteps of Freddie Gray. Despite the viral backlash, Graham defended her actions, stating she was simply looking out for her child amid escalating violence. She later expressed that she was angry he had made a decision to harm police officers, but emphasized her intent was to protect him.

Five Kurdish militants were killed and one wounded in clashes with Turkish forces in Agri, with four soldiers also injured. Turkish leaders, including Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, condemned the attack, which occurred ahead of a spring festival and followed a call from imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan for an end to the violence.

The USS Independence, a former U.S. Navy carrier scuttled in 1951, was found remarkably intact at the bottom of the Pacific. Researchers from NOAA used an underwater drone to survey the wreck, noting it sits upright and appears ready to launch its planes despite being submerged for 64 years. The ship survived a Japanese torpedo attack and was later positioned near ground zero for two atomic bomb tests, serving as a "guinea pig" for the dawn of the nuclear age.

A migrant capsized boat in the Mediterranean revealed that many were trapped below deck behind locked doors, causing a deadly panic as the vessel listed. The incident, which occurred about 110 kilometers north of Libya, resulted in at least 24 confirmed deaths and dozens rescued, with survivors reporting that smugglers had sealed the lower levels to prevent escape. The tragedy highlights the extreme dangers faced by migrants attempting the crossing, with the Italian Coast Guard continuing to collect statements as the death toll rises.

Creflo Dollar is defending his campaign to buy a $65 million Gulfstream G650 jet, arguing that critics misunderstand his ministry's needs after two accidents with his aging plane. He claims the fundraising effort, which seeks $300 from 200,000 people, is necessary for safe travel to spread his message globally, asserting that the devil is trying to discredit him.

The article argues that the highly anticipated Mayweather-Pacquiao fight is a symptom of boxing's decline rather than a revival, highlighting the sport's mismanagement and competition from MMA. It suggests that while fans are drawn to the visceral thrill of violence, their interest is more complex than simple bloodlust, contrasting the "tame" pay-per-view fights with extreme online violence. Ultimately, the piece posits that the enduring appeal of combat sports stems from a shared, guilty fascination with aggression that exists across all levels of society.

A bus carrying athletes collided with a fuel tanker in southern Morocco on Friday, resulting in a fire that killed at least 35 people, mostly children. The accident occurred near Tan-Tan just before 7 a.m., leaving the bus's frame hollowed out and scattering debris across the road. The dead included young athletes traveling for a sporting competition, and many others were injured in the crash.

Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro promised an apartment to Marleni Olivo after she threw a mango with her contact information at his bus during a rally in Anzoategui. Olivo, who was facing housing difficulties and health issues, intended only to leave a note for the president but instead became the unexpected recipient of a housing solution. Maduro humorously accepted the "gift," noting the mango's ripeness shared his name, and pledged to fulfill her housing request through the Great Housing Mission.

Attorney General Loretta Lynch faces the immediate challenge of restoring order in Baltimore following Freddie Gray's death, where she has pledged to deploy the full resources of the Justice Department to investigate wrongdoing and protect civil rights. To address systemic police abuse, Lynch plans to leverage the Justice Department's power to withhold federal funds from local departments that fail to reform, signaling a shift from encouragement to enforcement. This approach aims to compel better community relations and accountability in police departments nationwide, starting with a close examination of the Baltimore Police Department.

Ben Affleck successfully lobbied PBS's "Finding Your Roots" to remove references to his slave-owning ancestor, a request that producer Henry Louis Gates Jr. appears to have granted. The controversy resurfaced after leaked emails showed Gates agreeing with Affleck's desire to omit the "sins of an ancestor," though Gates later denied the request influenced the editing. The incident has prompted PBS to review its editorial standards regarding family history programming.

A helicopter crash in Malaysia on Saturday killed six people, including former ambassador Jamaluddin Jarjis and a high-ranking staff member of Prime Minister Najib Razak. Najib ordered an investigation, calling the victims "figures who had made great contributions to the government, party and country." The flight recorder was found in good condition, and authorities are expected to release a preliminary report within seven days.

President Obama reframed climate change as a public health issue during a roundtable at Howard University, emphasizing that rising temperatures increase heat-related illnesses and insect-borne diseases. He highlighted the success of the Clean Air Act in reducing respiratory ailments and urged citizens and medical professionals to pressure elected officials to mitigate climate impacts. Obama also proclaimed April 6–12 as National Public Health Week to raise awareness about these risks.

An Indonesian court rejected a legal challenge by Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, two members of the "Bali Nine" facing execution for a 2005 heroin smuggling plot. The judges ruled they lacked jurisdiction to challenge President Joko Widodo's refusal to grant clemency, effectively clearing the way for the scheduled executions.

Nick Loeb, Sofia Vergara's ex-fiancé, has filed a legal complaint to prevent the destruction of two frozen embryos they created together during their relationship. He argues that since he is willing to take on all parental responsibilities, he should be entitled to implant the embryos via a surrogate, despite the prior consent form requiring both parties' agreement. The case highlights the legal complexities surrounding embryo custody, as courts typically prioritize the egg donor's rights, but Loeb is challenging the enforceability of their agreement.

Six survivors of the January kosher supermarket siege are suing BFMTV, accusing the French news channel of endangering hostages by broadcasting their location live during the attack. The lawsuit, filed on March 27, alleges that a journalist mentioned the presence of a hidden woman, which the network immediately retracted to protect the hostages' safety. The legal action stems from the January 9 hostage-taking at the Hyper Cacher supermarket, which was part of a broader three-day terror attack that began with the Charlie Hebdo shooting.

President Barack Obama confirmed that a U.S. drone strike killed two aid workers held hostage by Al Qaeda on the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. The article highlights a pattern of rogue regimes seizing hostages during diplomatic overtures to extract concessions, citing the 1979 Iran hostage crisis as a historical precedent where seized diplomats were used to block U.S.-Iran reconciliation. The current detention of Jason Rezaian and other Iranian-Americans is framed as part of this enduring tactic of using captives to influence international negotiations.

The Slants, an Asian-American band, sought to trademark their name to reclaim a derogatory term, but the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office denied the registration under Section 2(a), which prohibits "disparaging" marks. The band argued that by owning the term, they empower themselves rather than perpetuate harm, drawing parallels to previous victories for groups like "Dykes on Bikes." However, the court's decision reflects a broader societal tendency to take offense easily, particularly given the ongoing controversy surrounding the Washington Redskins' trademark.

Italian navy commandos boarded a fishing boat off Sicily to retake it from gunmen who had seized it earlier, injuring one fisherman in the process. The incident occurred about 56 miles from Libya, with the boat carrying migrants from Sicily and Tunisia, highlighting the dangerous and volatile nature of migrant smuggling routes in the Mediterranean.

A gunman shot and killed a print shop operator at Wayne Community College in Goldsboro, North Carolina, before fleeing the scene. Authorities have placed the campus on lockdown and are actively searching for the suspect, who is described as "armed and dangerous." The victim, identified as Ron Lane, was a longtime employee, and the suspect, Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, is a former student and former employee of the college.

CNN's investigation reveals that smugglers in Libya lure migrants onto overcrowded boats by offering financial discounts for recruiting additional passengers. A recorded conversation shows that smugglers promise a free passage for those who bring 10 migrants, exploiting the desperation of those fleeing conflict and poverty. The report highlights the dangerous incentives driving the Mediterranean crossing, where an estimated 1,600 people have died this year alone.

Using seismic technology, University of Utah scientists have discovered that Yellowstone's magma reservoirs are far larger than previously thought, containing enough hot rock to fill the Grand Canyon nearly 14 times. While the discovery provides a crucial 3D map of the volcano's structure, researchers emphasize that the actual eruption hazard remains extremely low, with a 1 in 700,000 chance of an event in the next few thousand years.

Netflix has ordered a "Full House" reunion spinoff titled "Fuller House," featuring Candace Cameron Bure as a widowed mother of three, with John Stamos producing and guest starring. The series will see Jodie Sweetin and Andrea Barber return as Stephanie Tanner and Kimmy Gibbler, moving in to help D.J. Tanner raise her children in San Francisco. Talks are ongoing with other original cast members, including Bob Saget and the Olsen twins, with the show set to premiere next year.

Hungarian architect Matyas Gutai has developed a "liquid engineering" system where water trapped between panel layers equalizes a building's temperature, allowing it to reheat itself using stored energy. The prototype house in Kecskemet showcases this sustainable design, which reduces dependence on energy suppliers and carbon emissions by adapting to its environment rather than resisting it. While the system addresses freezing risks through natural solvents, Gutai views the project as a shift toward architecture that permanently adapts to its surroundings.

The U.S. has deployed warships to monitor Iranian vessels near Yemen, creating "options" to respond to potential arms transfers to Houthi rebels while ensuring safe shipping lanes. President Obama emphasized that the U.S. has issued direct warnings to Iran against delivering weapons that could threaten navigation. The move aims to reassure regional allies and monitor maritime traffic, though boarding Iranian ships would be an extraordinary step.

Shelling and aerial bombardment have gripped the Yemeni city of Aden, where residents face daily fear, scarcity, and the choice to stay indoors or risk death. Since Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes against Houthi rebels three weeks ago, the conflict has intensified, leaving the city's control divided and its population desperate for safety and supplies. Doctors have abandoned counting the dead, and both loyalist forces and civilians describe a terrifying reality where the war's human and material toll continues to mount.

A 54-year-old man was apprehended after scaling the White House fence and entering the South Lawn with a suspicious package on Sunday night. The Secret Service quickly detained the man, who was described as compliant, and the package was later deemed harmless. This incident adds to a series of recent security breaches at the White House, prompting calls for improved perimeter protection.

An Alaska Airlines flight bound for Los Angeles made an emergency landing in Seattle after a ramp agent fell asleep inside the front cargo hold. The agent, an employee of contractor Menzies Aviation, was found upon landing and taken to a hospital as a precaution before being discharged. All 170 passengers and crew eventually reached their destination after the plane resumed its flight.

The Baltimore Orioles' game against the Chicago White Sox on Wednesday was played without fans due to safety concerns following recent unrest and riots in the city. This decision marks a rare occurrence in Major League Baseball history, with officials citing the need to minimize safety risks while the league and local leaders monitor the tense situation. The Orioles have postponed several games and relocated others to Florida as they navigate the ongoing instability in Baltimore.

The Kentucky Wildcats' undefeated season ended with a 71-64 loss to the Wisconsin Badgers in the NCAA Final Four, who overcame a late deficit to advance to the championship game. Freshman Karl-Anthony Towns led Kentucky with 16 points, but the Badgers' balanced attack, spearheaded by Frank Kaminsky's 20 points and 11 rebounds, proved too much for the Wildcats to handle. Wisconsin will face Duke in the title game after the Blue Devils defeated Michigan State 81-61.

Judge Jeffrey Sutton authored the only recent appellate court decision upholding state bans on same-sex marriage, arguing that the issue should be left to the democratic process rather than judicial interpretation. His opinion, which frames same-sex marriage as a matter for citizens to decide rather than a constitutional right, stands in stark contrast to the majority of courts that have struck down such bans. The ruling is significant as it provides the legal framework expected to be used by states defending their bans before the U.S. Supreme Court.

New Belgium Brewery and Ben & Jerry's are collaborating on a salted caramel brownie ice cream-inspired beer to raise awareness for social and environmental causes. The companies, both certified B Corporations, plan to launch the product in the fall, though specific campaign details remain under wraps. The partnership highlights the shared values of the two brands, which have a history of activism on issues like climate change and marriage equality.

The NASA MESSENGER spacecraft is set to crash onto Mercury around April 30 after running out of fuel, concluding a mission that provided the first detailed data about the planet's composition and revealed ice in its polar regions. Despite efforts to extend its orbit using remaining fuel, the probe will impact the surface at high speed on the side facing away from Earth, marking the end of its 11-year study of the solar system's innermost planet.

Saudi airstrikes resumed in Yemen after Houthi rebels attacked a government military brigade, despite the U.N.-sponsored peace talks being called off unless attacks cease. The renewed bombing, which targeted a weapons depot in Taiz, follows the release of Yemen's Defense Minister by the Houthis, but the conflict escalation threatens to derail ongoing diplomatic efforts.

Xenophobic violence has erupted in South Africa, resulting in at least six deaths and prompting other African nations to evacuate their citizens. The attacks, which have occurred in waves since 2006, were sparked by remarks from traditional leaders and fueled by high unemployment and resentment toward immigrants. While President Jacob Zuma acknowledges the economic concerns driving the unrest, he maintains that immigrants contribute positively to the country and should not be stereotyped as criminals.

The article discusses how the publicized beheadings by ISIS have created a "copy-cat" effect, potentially inspiring similar acts by both extremists and non-extremists. Psychology professor Arie Kruglanski suggests that the frequent media coverage of these killings "primes" individuals to emulate the violence during times of stress. While reports of beheadings have surfaced globally—from Saudi Arabia to Mexico—the ISIS propaganda has uniquely amplified the practice, making the threat of decapitation a more immediate psychological concern worldwide.

Bobbi Kristina Brown, the daughter of Bobby Brown and Whitney Houston, remains in a "global and irreversible brain damage" state despite her father's claims she is awake. Her grandmother, Cissy Houston, stated that Bobbi Kristina is unresponsive and on a long-term rehabilitation path, with her future quality of life uncertain. Doctors have indicated she will live a long life, but her current condition requires ongoing care.

James Holmes opened fire during a midnight screening of "The Dark Knight Rises" in Aurora, Colorado, in 2012, killing 12 and injuring 70. He has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, claiming he was suffering a psychotic episode, while prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. The trial, which began with jury selection in January, could last until autumn as Holmes, a former neuroscience doctoral student, faces 165 counts.

A U.S. Army soldier was killed and others were injured in an attack at a provincial governor's compound in Jalalabad, Afghanistan, where an Afghan National Army gunman opened fire on U.S. troops. The incident occurred shortly after a senior U.S. official met with the governor, and while the motive remains unclear, a senior U.S. analyst noted that "green-on-blue" attacks have been declining due to fewer U.S. troops and improved vetting of Afghan forces.

A white police officer in North Charleston was charged with murder after raw video surfaced showing him shooting an unarmed black man in the back as he fled a traffic stop. The footage contradicts the officer's initial claim that he felt threatened, and the case has sparked national outrage due to the clear visual evidence contradicting the official account. Activists and family members emphasize that without the bystander video, the shooting would likely have been ruled justifiable, highlighting broader concerns about police use of force against Black men.

The article details the ongoing migration crisis from North Africa to Italy, noting that over 10,000 people have arrived in Sicily since last weekend alone. It traces the historical context of the flow, explaining that under Muammar Gaddafi's rule, migration was tightly controlled, but after his overthrow in 2011, the numbers surged, resulting in thousands of deaths. The piece highlights Italy's various rescue efforts, from the Mare Nostrum operation to the current EU mission Triton, emphasizing the dangerous and unregulated nature of the crossings.

Photographer James Oatway captured the fatal attack on Mozambican national Emmanuel Sithole in Alexandra Township, where he was bludgeoned and stabbed by a mob in broad daylight. Despite Oatway's efforts to intervene, Sithole died from his injuries, and the haunting images sparked national outrage, appearing on the front page of the Sunday Times. The violence is part of a broader surge in xenophobic attacks across South Africa, fueled by economic tensions and inflammatory rhetoric from local leaders.

The death of Freddie Gray sparked Baltimore riots and renewed scrutiny of police use of force. Gray died after sustaining severe spinal injuries while in police custody, with his family alleging he was not properly secured in the van. Authorities and the Justice Department are investigating, with the case centering on whether the stop and subsequent arrest were legally justified based on Gray's flight and the presence of a knife.

Kenyan authorities have identified Mohamed Mohamud, also known as Dulyadin, as the mastermind behind the Garissa University College attack, crediting him with an extensive network within the country and the Dadaab refugee camp. Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the assault, which killed over 147 people, while the government continues to pursue other suspects, including Abdirahim Abdullahi, whose father publicly appealed for information regarding his whereabouts.

Following a preliminary nuclear framework between Iran and world powers, the Iranian public expresses optimism about sanctions relief and improved international relations, while the military celebrates National Army Day by framing the armed forces as regional peacemakers. Despite this hopeful tone, top officials maintain hardline rhetoric, with the Chief of Staff urging U.S.-Iran cooperation against ISIS and dismissing American intelligence efforts. The article highlights a contrast between the public's desire for peace and the government's continued assertion of military strength and regional dominance.

The debate over the word "thug" intensified after President Obama and Baltimore Mayor Rawlings-Blake used it to describe rioters, with critics arguing it serves as a modern racial slur equivalent to the N-word. Rev. Jamal Bryant and Councilman Carl Stokes condemned the term, asserting it dehumanizes frustrated youth while officials like Kweisi Mfume emphasize that labeling them is less important than addressing the underlying poverty and unrest. The controversy stems from the unrest following Freddie Gray's death, with figures like Kevin Shird acknowledging the term's racialized impact in America despite personal disagreements on its

Mehmet Oz weathered a coordinated attack from 10 colleagues who accused him of promoting "quack treatments" for financial gain, but he successfully deflected the criticism by exposing their motives and highlighting his own academic standing. Despite the Senate's previous humiliation and a scathing takedown by John Oliver, Columbia University and its affiliated hospital have stood by Oz, choosing to retain him rather than sever ties. The doctors' attempt to oust him backfired, ultimately reinforcing Oz's position while drawing further attention to the medical and media establishment's tolerance of his controversial methods.

Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, a top leader of Lashkar-e-Taiba accused of masterminding the 2008 Mumbai attacks, was released on bail in Pakistan on Thursday, drawing sharp condemnation from India. India's Ministry of External Affairs criticized the release, arguing it reinforced the perception of a "dual policy" regarding terrorists targeting India, while Pakistan's Foreign Office defended the decision, blaming India's lack of cooperation for weakening the prosecution.

A California woman was terrified when a U.S. marshal grabbed her phone and smashed it while she was recording a police activity from a distance. The incident was captured on video by a neighbor, and the woman is now considering a lawsuit, arguing she had a right to record. The U.S. Marshals Service is reviewing the incident, and a local representative has called for a federal investigation.

Novak Djokovic extended his winning streak to 17 matches by defeating Thomas Berdych 7-5, 4-6, 6-3 in the rain-interrupted Monte Carlo Masters final. Despite losing the second set, Djokovic broke Berdych twice early in the third set to surge to a 4-0 lead and secure the title. The victory marked Djokovic's 52nd career title and his second Monte Carlo Masters championship, completing a rare sweep of the opening three Masters tournaments of the 2015 season.

Suzanne Crough, who played the youngest daughter Tracy on "The Partridge Family," has died at age 52. She passed away at her home in Laughlin, Nevada, and is remembered for her role in the iconic '70s musical sitcom alongside her TV siblings.

Muhammadu Buhari's victory marks a historic, peaceful transition of power in Nigeria, signaling a shift away from the entrenched corruption of the previous administration. His win, running on an anti-corruption platform, reflects the public's frustration with economic hardship and the collapse of the oil-dependent status quo. However, the transition occurs against a backdrop of severe security challenges, including Boko Haram's insurgency and deep religious and ethnic divides.

A draft script for "The Breakfast Club" was discovered in a Maine Township High School District filing cabinet, revealing that Molly Ringwald's character was originally named Cathy Douglas. The manuscript, dated September 1983 and signed by the district's former superintendent, highlights the film's deep roots at Maine North High School. District officials are now hoping to display the script as a piece of local and cinematic history.

An Egyptian court sentenced Mohamed Badie, the leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, and 13 others to death by hanging, while 36 more received life sentences for plotting attacks and supporting former President Morsy. The sentencing of U.S.-Egyptian activist Mohamad Soltan, who has been on a 14-month hunger strike, drew condemnation from the U.S. State Department.

Tuesday marks Equal Pay Day, a progressive holiday highlighting the wage gap, which gained new urgency following Hillary Clinton's presidential announcement. However, the widely cited 77-cent statistic is misleading as it compares averages without controlling for key factors like profession and hours worked; when adjusted, the gap narrows to roughly 4-6 cents, largely due to individual choices rather than systemic discrimination. Despite this, Democrats are expected to make workplace equity a central issue in the upcoming election, arguing that a persistent 5-point gender gap favors them and that Republicans risk political backlash if they oppose pay equity measures.

Following the death of Freddie Gray and subsequent unrest in Baltimore, MLB postponed two games against the Chicago White Sox due to "ongoing public safety issues." This decision echoed historical precedents where sports were halted during civil unrest, such as the 1967 Detroit riots and the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination. While officials hoped the pause would address safety concerns, the situation highlighted the tension between sports and broader social turmoil.

"Monty Python and the Holy Grail," released 40 years ago, began as a low-budget production plagued by technical issues and Chapman's alcohol withdrawal, but it became a massive hit thanks to word-of-mouth and TV popularity. The film is widely considered the most consistent and quotable of the Python movies, celebrated for its absurd gags like the Black Knight and the Knights Who Say "Ni," and it launched the successful Broadway spin-off "Spamalot."

Jeff Green's career was nearly ended by an aortic aneurysm discovered during a routine physical, forcing him to miss the entire 2011-2012 season and undergo open heart surgery. After focusing on his education at Georgetown to prepare for life after basketball, he slowly recovered and returned to the NBA with a new perspective, now using his experience to raise awareness about hidden heart risks.

Police brutality against unarmed African-Americans is a decades-long issue that has become a national crisis, exacerbated by the loss of public confidence in law enforcement. While the rise of cell phone cameras and social media has finally brought these incidents to light, ending the violence requires sustained, targeted training and accountability to address deep-seated cultural norms within policing.

A Chinese court convicted veteran journalist Gao Yu of revealing state secrets and sentenced her to seven years in prison, a verdict her lawyer called "wrong" and based on a retracted, forced confession. The 71-year-old journalist, who was detained ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Tiananmen Square crackdown, plans to appeal the ruling, which rights groups say is part of a broader crackdown under President Xi Jinping.

New York state authorities have issued a health alert after over 160 patients were hospitalized in nine days due to synthetic marijuana emergencies. Officials warn that the drugs, often marketed as incense, are dangerous and can cause severe, long-term brain damage, with similar spikes reported in Alabama and Mississippi.

Amy Schumer dominated the entertainment headlines this week with a series of bold antics. She stole the spotlight at the TIME 100 gala by faking a tumble in front of Kanye West and Kim Kardashian, and later shocked David Letterman by lifting her dress to reveal a surfing scar on her vagina. The comedian’s "moment" was capped by the premiere of her show's third season and a renewal for a fourth.

Hillary Clinton officially launched her 2016 presidential campaign, sparking an immediate and massive social media response. The announcement generated millions of views and trending hashtags across Twitter and Facebook, reflecting both strong support and significant criticism from the public.

Julian Assange has agreed to be interviewed by Swedish prosecutors at the Ecuadorian Embassy in London, ending his refusal to travel to Sweden. This move comes as prosecutors face a deadline before the statute of limitations expires on the 2010 sexual assault allegations against him. While Assange maintains his innocence and fears extradition to the U.S., the interview represents a significant shift in the investigation's approach.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, Chinese nuclear experts have told the U.S. that North Korea may already possess up to 20 nuclear warheads, but the more alarming development is the prediction that Pyongyang could double this arsenal by next year using highly-enriched uranium. This assessment suggests North Korea could rapidly expand its stockpile to around 40 warheads, potentially rendering past plutonium-focused negotiations trivial and indicating a "runaway" weapons program fueled by domestic uranium mines. The report underscores that the threat from North Korea may have been consistently downplayed,

A new microneedle patch technology could be the key to finally eradicating polio by enabling minimally trained personnel to easily administer vaccines door-to-door, bypassing the logistical challenges of traditional needles. This innovation arrives as the world nears eradication, though polio remains endemic in a few regions, with the U.S. having successfully eliminated the disease since the 1950s through widespread vaccination efforts. The patch represents a significant advancement in delivery, potentially allowing vaccines to reach remote or conflict-affected areas where current methods have failed.

Myopia rates have surged globally, particularly in East Asia where up to 96% of young adults are affected, driven largely by a lack of outdoor time rather than excessive studying. Researchers emphasize that increased sunlight exposure during childhood development is the most effective prevention, though cultural and educational pressures make implementing outdoor time difficult.

Hillary Clinton announced she would take a 23% pay cut if elected president to highlight the gender wage gap, arguing that women earn 77 cents for every dollar men make. The article frames this as a political stunt to position Clinton as a populist champion, though it questions whether her wealth and background align with the working women she aims to represent.

Two TSA screeners were fired after a male officer allegedly conspired with a female colleague to grope attractive men by manipulating the screening machine to trigger false anomalies. The scheme was uncovered when an investigator observed the plan being carried out in February, and the female officer admitted to repeating the act at least 10 times. The TSA called the incident "egregious and intolerable," but no criminal charges are expected due to the lack of an identifiable victim.

Newly revised NYPD training materials, submitted to a federal judge for approval, would require new cadets to avoid racial profiling, ethnic jokes, and stereotyping. The 140-page update, crafted with court-appointed monitor Peter Zimroth, responds to a 2013 ruling that found the "Stop, Question and Frisk" practice unconstitutional. The training aims to foster respectful community partnerships while ensuring officers lawfully conduct stops and engage with the public without bias.

Iran's President Hassan Rouhani stated that a final nuclear deal will only be signed if all economic sanctions are lifted on the first day of implementation. Meanwhile, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei refrained from taking a position, citing that the deal is not yet final and warning that the U.S. might backtrack on specifics. Negotiators have until June 30 to finalize the agreement, with Rouhani insisting his government will not surrender to what he called "bullying" and "threats."

Falih Essawi, a local official, warned that ISIS militants are hours away from capturing Ramadi, the capital of Anbar province, as government forces struggle to hold their lines. He reported that at least 10 security forces were killed and over 100 wounded on Wednesday, while over 150,000 residents have fled the city amid fierce fighting and collapsing security. Essawi urgently pleaded for military reinforcements and U.S.-led airstrikes to prevent the city's fall.

A group of American citizens, including Muna Mansour and her nine family members, are trapped in Yemen's port city of Aden with limited resources, despite the ongoing conflict between Houthi rebels and government forces. While other nations like India have successfully evacuated their citizens, the U.S. State Department has refused direct evacuation, citing the "dangerous and unpredictable" security situation. The family has been waiting at the port for weeks, running out of food and money, and has filed a lawsuit against the State and Defense Departments to demand their evacuation.

The article explains that a postal carrier from Florida landed a gyrocopter on Capitol grounds, breaching the highly restricted Washington D.C. Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA). The author notes that the pilot likely exploited the fact that gyrocopters require a ground run for takeoff and may have weighed under 255 pounds, allowing him to bypass standard SFRA restrictions designed for larger aircraft. The incident highlights the serious security vulnerabilities in restricted airspace, where noncompliance can lead to severe federal penalties, including the interception of the aircraft by F-16s.

New research based on a year of data from the Curiosity rover suggests that salty water may form in tiny puddles on Mars at night, though the conditions are still too harsh to support life as we know it. While the study strengthens the theory that brines could exist across the planet, it doesn't change the fact that Mars remains an overwhelmingly dry and inhospitable place today. Scientists continue to search for evidence of past life, focusing on the planet's history of liquid water and ice at the poles.

The Shanghai Auto Show has banned "car babes" to shift focus toward vehicle displays, highlighting a competitive market where global and local automakers are vying for Chinese consumers. With sales nearing 23.5 million units last year, the event showcases new models catering to local preferences, particularly the rising demand for SUVs, while Chinese brands like Geely aim to expand into developed markets like the U.S.

Thailand has replaced martial law with a new security order granting the military junta sweeping, unchecked powers to detain, censor media, and restrict political gatherings. Human rights groups and the UN have condemned the move, warning it effectively institutionalizes dictatorship and undermines the junta's promise to restore democracy. The new measures allow Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha to rule by decree without judicial oversight, sparking alarm over the future of civil liberties in the country.

David Letterman's final "Late Show" will air on May 20, featuring a star-studded farewell lineup including Oprah Winfrey, George Clooney, Jerry Seinfeld, and Bill Murray. The episode will also welcome back old friends like Michael Keaton and Ray Romano, marking the end of Letterman's 33-year late-night career before Stephen Colbert takes over the show in September.

A massive brawl involving two dozen people broke out at Resorts World Casino in Queens, New York, on Friday night, captured on cell phone video showing patrons throwing punches and chairs. The chaos, which occurred in the food court in front of a newly opened Fat Tuesday, resulted in several thousand dollars in damages and three arrests, with one man charged with obstructing governmental administration. Police are still investigating the cause of the fight, which they described as resembling a "World Wrestling Entertainment event."

The $16 million Mary Harvin Transformation Center, a community hub planned to revitalize a blighted East Baltimore neighborhood, was destroyed by fire during riots following Freddie Gray's funeral. Local leaders expressed dismay but vowed to rebuild, viewing the center as essential to addressing long-standing issues like poverty, unemployment, and failing schools. The cause of the blaze remains under investigation, though anger over Gray's death and systemic social issues are cited as contributing factors.

Saudi Arabia, backed by U.S. intelligence and weaponry, launched airstrikes in Yemen to "restore the legitimate government," but the move is widely seen as a bid to prevent the rise of popularly supported, self-determining governments in the region. The Obama administration's alignment with Saudi ambitions effectively ceded Yemeni control to Riyadh, prioritizing Saudi interests over the previous American goal of dismantling al Qaeda's safe haven. This shift is criticized as misguided, given that the Houthis—despite Iranian support—have not targeted U.S. interests

A Somali woman's seven-month journey to Libya ended in detention, where she gave birth to her baby, Sabrine, a week later. Along with 350 other migrants, she is now stranded in a facility outside Tripoli as Libyan officials struggle to determine their fate. The crisis was underscored by a recent shipwreck off Malta, where 24 bodies were recovered from a capsized vessel, highlighting the deadly risks migrants face while seeking a better life in Europe.

A massive avalanche triggered by the Nepal earthquake struck Everest Base Camp, killing at least 17 people and injuring dozens. Stranded climbers at higher camps are awaiting rescue, but the Khumbu Icefall has been deemed impassable due to ongoing aftershocks. Helicopters are working to evacuate those trapped, with estimates suggesting hundreds remain on the mountain.

Former New England Patriots star Aaron Hernandez was sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2013 murder of Odin Lloyd, a conviction that erased his $40 million contract and marked a dramatic fall from grace. Despite Hernandez's claims of innocence, the jury found him guilty of first-degree murder, and Lloyd's mother expressed forgiveness toward those involved in her son's death. The case concluded with the district attorney emphasizing that Hernandez, now a convicted citizen, must answer for his "depraved conduct."

The University of Florida and Emory University are investigating Zeta Beta Tau fraternity members for allegedly spitting, urinating, and pouring beer on wounded war veterans and their service dogs at a Panama City Beach resort. The fraternity's international office has suspended chapters at both schools and expelled three members from the University of Florida, issuing a public apology for the "unacceptable behavior." University and fraternity officials alike have condemned the actions, stating they do not represent the values of the institutions or the organization.

The author recounts her journey to becoming a triathlete, highlighting how partnering up with friends helped her stay accountable through the winter. She details her first marathon experience in Arkansas with fellow racers and her transition to outdoor cycling with a local club, crediting her fitness community for keeping her motivated.

After over nine years and 3 billion miles of travel, NASA's New Horizons spacecraft has sent back its first color image of Pluto and its moon Charon. The probe is set to make its historic closest approach on July 14, promising to transform distant points of light into a detailed portrait of the dwarf planet and the unexplored Kuiper Belt.

On April 12, 1945, the death of President Franklin D. Roosevelt triggered immediate chaos at the Chicago Daily News. As the news broke, staff scrambled to clear the desks and rush to the railroad terminal to cover the anticipated public reaction. With only an hour remaining before the afternoon paper went to press, reporters frantically gathered information to meet the EXTRA deadline.

Jihadi groups like ISIS and Boko Haram systematically target women not just for violence, but as a calculated strategy to build "caliphates" by forcing conversion, sexual slavery, and subjugation. Unlike previous groups like al Qaeda, which viewed establishing a religious state as a distant goal, ISIS actively creates social structures through the organized abuse of women to ensure the group's survival and expansion. Human Rights Watch and other organizations have documented these acts as war crimes and crimes against humanity, highlighting the deliberate use of women as tools for ideological and demographic control.

Government officials are investigating a potential misuse of the banned pesticide methyl bromide in the U.S. Virgin Islands, following a family's vacation that turned into a medical emergency. At least two brothers remain in comas after staying at the Sirenusa resort, where authorities found evidence the pesticide was used improperly multiple times. Officials are working to track down other vacationers who may have been exposed, as the pesticide is illegal for indoor use and was reportedly used by companies like Terminix across the islands.

Researchers extracted DNA from the Altamura Man, the oldest Neanderthal ever discovered, after over two decades of study. The 128,000 to 187,000-year-old remains were found in a cave in Italy, where the hominid likely fell into a well and died of thirst or hunger. Scientists hope the DNA will provide new insights into human evolution and Neanderthal life in Europe.

ISIS is a brutal organization driven by a mix of radical religious ideology and a lust for power, largely composed of former Saddam Hussein officers rather than pure zealots. While the group has gained ground by exploiting Sunni rebellion against Shiite rule, its harsh theocratic rule is generating internal discontent and fear, suggesting it may ultimately be undone by the very populations it oppresses.

Pope Francis will visit Cuba in September before traveling to the U.S., marking a significant stop during his trip that follows his role in normalizing U.S.-Cuba relations. The Vatican announced the visit as a gesture of goodwill, with the Pope expected to stop in Havana before addressing Congress and the U.N. in Washington and New York.

Hillary Clinton has officially launched her second presidential campaign, joining a crowded Democratic field and continuing a political legacy that has spanned nearly a quarter-century. While she remains the most recognizable candidate, her run is complicated by a mixed record on foreign policy and criticism that her ties to corporate interests undermine her credibility as a fighter for economic equality. As she attempts to distance herself from the Clinton Foundation and defend her tenure at the State Department, Clinton faces the challenge of defining her platform in a party energized by issues of inequality and reform.

A&E, Lifetime, and History are simulcasting a 2016 remake of the 1977 miniseries "Roots," co-executive produced by LeVar Burton. The new version aims to introduce the story of Kunta Kinte to a new generation, consulting historians for accuracy amid modern racial discourse.

The article argues that the unrest in Baltimore is a collective responsibility, asserting that "we" are the authors of the city's story due to a legacy of racial and economic inequality. It critiques how both liberals and conservatives use the riots to confirm their pre-existing political biases rather than address systemic issues. Ultimately, the piece contends that acknowledging this shared history of injustice is necessary before any meaningful change can occur.

In July 2013, Turkish archaeologists discovered a stone chest in a 1,350-year-old church that appeared to contain a piece of Jesus' cross, but the find stalled when the box was found mysteriously empty. The episode highlights the broader "true cross" phenomenon, which began with Saint Helena's 4th-century search for relics and has since been plagued by questions of authenticity, as scholars debate whether surviving fragments are genuine or forgeries born of the faithful's desire to believe.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 is set to expand to cover a new area of the southern Indian Ocean, doubling the current search zone to over 120,000 square kilometers. If the current 60,000-square-kilometer priority zone is completed without finding the plane, the expanded search could take up to a year to finish. Officials from Malaysia, Australia, and China remain committed to finding the aircraft to bring closure to the families of the 239 people on board.

As protests erupted nationwide following Freddie Gray's death, Charmington's cafe in Baltimore closed temporarily to allow staff to support the community through cleanup and peaceful protest. The closure was an act of solidarity for the "Black Lives Matter" movement and local businesses affected by the rioting, with staff like Mike Dobson providing free food and water to demonstrators. While some businesses like Trevira London's boutique suffered significant damage, the atmosphere in Baltimore has shifted toward peaceful celebration and community support.

DC Entertainment, Warner Bros., and Mattel have partnered to launch "DC Super Hero Girls," a new franchise targeting girls aged 6-12 through toys, books, and TV specials featuring teenaged versions of characters like Wonder Woman and Supergirl. While some social media users welcomed the initiative, others criticized it as exclusionary, arguing it reinforces gender divides rather than integrating female heroes into the broader universe. The first elements of the franchise are set to roll out in the fall.

Five years after the Deepwater Horizon disaster, the Gulf of Mexico continues to grapple with the spill's legacy, as oil remains on the seafloor and communities still face economic and environmental devastation. While progress has been made in restoration efforts, significant safety reforms recommended after the spill have yet to be fully implemented, leaving the region vulnerable to future catastrophes. The article underscores that despite assurances of recovery, the environmental and human toll of the BP spill remains an open wound rather than a closed chapter.

Henry Louis Gates Jr. edited Ben Affleck out of a segment about his slaveholding ancestor in the PBS series "Finding Your Roots," reportedly at Affleck's request to avoid "embarrassing" family history. While Gates claimed the edit was for "compelling television," the incident highlights a broader reluctance to confront the legacy of slavery, especially given Affleck's public support for foreign aid while avoiding his own familial ties to the institution. The controversy underscores the tension between privacy, historical truth, and the media's role in shaping narratives about America's racial past.

A white police officer in North Charleston shot and killed an unarmed black man, Walter Scott, after stopping him for a broken taillight; the killing was captured on video showing the officer firing at Scott as he fled, leading to his arrest on murder charges. The incident sparked outrage in the predominantly black community, highlighting ongoing tensions between police and black citizens, and drawing comparisons to the Ferguson case where video evidence similarly exposed racial disparities in policing.

Hillary Clinton launched her 2016 presidential campaign with a low-key video featuring diverse women, deliberately shifting focus away from herself to emphasize a collective message of opportunity and breaking barriers. By highlighting the experiences of everyday Americans and leveraging a favorable political climate for women, Clinton positions herself as a champion for progress while navigating the challenge of generating excitement for a historic candidacy. The article notes that while Americans are broadly ready for a woman president, support splits along party lines, making her path to the nomination both timely and politically complex.

Ibrahim al-Rubaish, a former Guantanamo Bay detainee and senior al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula leader, was killed in a Yemeni airstrike on Monday. His death highlights the group's continued vulnerability despite the ongoing civil war and prison breaks that have released other senior figures.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren reiterated she is not running for president but described a candidate who would fight for the middle class and reform Washington, specifically criticizing Ted Cruz and Rand Paul for opposing student loan and Social Security benefits. She expressed a desire to see all candidates present their agendas but ruled out supporting those who vote against policies benefiting working families. While many liberals want her to challenge Hillary Clinton, Warren indicated she is waiting to see who else enters the race before making a decision.

A Colorado jury will begin deliberations on Monday in the trial of James Holmes, who pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity for the 2012 Aurora theater shooting that killed 12 and wounded 70. The prosecution is seeking the death penalty, while the defense argues Holmes was in a psychotic episode during the attack. Jurors will weigh evidence of Holmes' planning and mental state as they determine his fate.

SpaceX attempted to launch a Falcon 9 rocket carrying a cargo spacecraft to the International Space Station on Tuesday after scrubbing Monday's attempt due to weather. The mission's highlight will be the company's first attempt to land the rocket's first stage upright on a floating platform in the Atlantic Ocean, a feat SpaceX hopes will drastically reduce the cost of space travel. If successful, the Dragon spacecraft will deliver over 4,300 pounds of supplies and an espresso maker to the space station crew.

A CNN team traveled from Djibouti to Aden, Yemen, taking a longer, safer route to avoid conflict zones. After a difficult journey marked by rough seas and delays, they arrived to find a city under siege, witnessing frantic crowds and heavy shelling. With only five hours on the ground, the team attempted to document the humanitarian crisis before fleeing the port as fighting intensified, ultimately agreeing to evacuate 60 refugees despite an unfair "exit fee."

Jamal al-Labani, a U.S. citizen and gas station owner from California, was killed by mortar shrapnel in Aden, Yemen, becoming the first American fatality in the current conflict. His family had attempted to evacuate him as the situation deteriorated, but he was trapped as airports closed and violence escalated between Houthi rebels and Saudi-led airstrikes. The U.S. State Department has declined to evacuate private citizens, urging them to shelter in place despite the worsening crisis.

The Supreme Court is poised to rule on same-sex marriage, a case where public opinion has shifted dramatically since the issue first emerged in 2003. While originalists like Justice Scalia argue the Constitution does not guarantee such a right, the Court has historically been influenced by evolving social norms and global context rather than solely the framers' original intent.

A Syrian migrant, having lost his job and fearing persecution at home, paid a smuggler $6,500 to cross the Mediterranean to Italy. After a harrowing journey involving a nighttime walk through rough terrain and days waiting at sea, he finally reached Europe, where he now considers his life significantly better than it was before.

During his annual Q&A session, Vladimir Putin dismissed Western sanctions as an attempt to constrain Russia's development, defending the sale of advanced weapons to Iran while downplaying regional threats. The event, which saw a record number of public questions, was largely seen as a choreographed platform for the president rather than a genuine exchange, though it featured a surprise video link from Edward Snowden.

A listeria outbreak linked to Blue Bell Creameries has resulted in a full product recall across 23 states, with three deaths and 10 illnesses reported since January 2010. The CDC connected the cases through DNA testing, suggesting the bacteria may have persisted in the factory for years, though the exact source remains unknown.

A group of 10 physicians have accused Dr. Mehmet Oz of "manifesting an egregious lack of integrity" for promoting unproven treatments and have called for his removal from his faculty position at Columbia University. In response, Oz defends his work by stating he provides multiple viewpoints to help the public and will not be silenced, insisting he does not claim GMO foods are dangerous but supports labeling them. The controversy stems from concerns that Oz prioritizes personal financial gain over evidence-based medicine, particularly regarding genetically modified foods and weight loss products.

A passenger was killed and the driver was hospitalized with minor injuries after a Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at the Exotic Driving Experience at Walt Disney World Speedway on Sunday. The driver, Tavon Watson, lost control of the vehicle, and the 36-year-old passenger, Gary Terry, was pronounced dead at the scene. Petty Holdings, which operates the attraction, expressed deep sympathies to those involved in the tragic accident.

Eighteen-month-old twins Silas and Eli Keslar drowned after their mother, Alexis Keslar, let go of their stroller to fend off a bee, causing it to roll into a canal in Yuma, Arizona. Despite her efforts to rescue them, the steep sides and strong current of the waterway prevented her from saving the boys, who were later recovered after a lengthy search. Authorities emphasized the danger of the canals, noting that the swift current and steep embankments make them hazardous for those unfamiliar with the area.

A massive tornado touched down near Dallas on Sunday, causing significant damage to Rio Vista and Grandview with reports of ripped-off roofs and flipped 18-wheelers. While the storm produced awe-inspiring funnel clouds and hail the size of softballs, authorities confirmed no deaths or injuries, though damage assessments were delayed due to severe weather.

Pro-democracy legislators in Hong Kong have vowed to veto a Beijing-backed election proposal, arguing it falls short of true universal suffrage because candidates must be vetted by a pro-China committee. Chief Secretary Carrie Lam defended the plan as a step toward 2017 voting rights, but protesters and opposition lawmakers view it as a "ridiculous" sham that maintains Beijing's control. If the veto succeeds, the reform process will restart, potentially delaying Hong Kong's promised political changes indefinitely.

Australia recalled its ambassador to Indonesia following the execution of two Australian citizens, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, whom Prime Minister Tony Abbott described as "fully rehabilitated." The executions, which also included six other nationals and a Brazilian with a psychiatric condition, have strained relations, though Indonesia's President Joko Widodo defended the actions as upholding legal sovereignty. Philippines embassy officials confirmed that Mary Jane Veloso, a Filipino woman initially scheduled for execution, was spared at the last moment.

Toya Graham became a viral sensation after pulling her son away from a Baltimore riot, sparking debate over whether her physical reaction promoted or prevented violence. While critics questioned if her actions condoned aggression, supporters view her as a protective "momma bear" acting out of a desperate need to guide her child through a dangerous situation. Ultimately, the incident highlights the complex reality of parenting in volatile communities, where mothers like Graham are forced to make split-second decisions to keep their children safe.

Negotiators in Lausanne reached a significant framework to limit Iran's nuclear program, requiring a 98% reduction in low-enriched uranium and scaled-back centrifuges in exchange for the lifting of economic sanctions. While President Obama hailed the deal as cutting off Iran's pathways to a nuclear weapon, key details remain to be finalized, and both sides have stressed that the agreement is contingent on strict verification and the phased removal of sanctions.

This article is the second installment of a Catholic writer's journey reading the Bible from cover to cover, focusing on Genesis chapters 1–11. The author highlights the text's focus on the relationship between Earth and humanity, noting the surprising absence of Seth in popular memory and the intriguing mythology behind the "sons of heaven" taking wives.

Lee Min-bok, a North Korean defector, launches anti-regime propaganda balloons carrying copies of "The Interview" from South Korea to North Korea, despite the film's controversial depiction of Kim Jong Un's assassination and the risk of confrontation. He views the effort as a necessary act of truth-telling to challenge the regime's propaganda, acknowledging the danger but believing the truth will eventually seep through to North Korean citizens. The launches occur at night to avoid detection, though they draw ire from both North Korean forces and South Korean residents living near the border.

Australian police have charged a second individual in an "ISIS-inspired" terror plot, following the arrest of five young men in Melbourne. The suspects were allegedly planning attacks during Anzac Day commemorations, with one 18-year-old denied bail and others released pending further inquiries. Authorities emphasized the men acted alone and were not representative of any religious or cultural group.

A suicide bomber killed 17 people and wounded dozens, including an Afghan lawmaker, near protesters in Khost, eastern Afghanistan, on Thursday. The attack occurred as demonstrators were heading to a rally against the provincial governor, though the Taliban denied responsibility. No group has yet claimed the assault.

Conor McDonnell, a 23-year-old self-taught photographer, captured the most-liked Instagram photo to date with his shot of Kim and Kanye West's wedding embrace. Since posting his first photo in 2011, McDonnell has snapped global stars like Drake and Justin Bieber while traveling the world on private planes. He recently shared his top tips for Instagram success, emphasizing natural lighting, the rule of thirds, and strategic editing using apps like Snapseed and VSCO Cam.

An Arizona police officer intentionally struck an armed suspect with his patrol car after determining he was too far away to safely take a shot without endangering bystanders. The officer, Michael Rapiejko, stated he chose to use his vehicle as a weapon to stop the threat posed by Mario Valencia, who was walking through a business park with a rifle. Valencia survived the impact and faces multiple charges, while the department and officials have defended the officer's actions as justified given the suspect's armed status and the presence of civilians.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), set to launch in 2018, is designed to study the first galaxies and search for signs of life, acting as the successor to the Hubble Space Telescope. With a massive mirror and a golf ball of gold to optimize infrared vision, the $8.5 billion mission will peer back 13 billion years to observe the early universe and detect distant planets. Czech politician Vit Jedlicka has founded Liberland, a new micronation on a disputed 7-square-kilometer patch of land between Serbia and Croatia. Declaring it a libertarian "constitutional republic," he plans to formally establish the country on May 1 and has invited 7,500 of the 300,000 citizenship applicants to the ceremony. The nation prides itself on minimal government interference, using cryptocurrency and guaranteeing personal and economic freedom to its future residents.

On April 9, 1865, Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Courthouse, effectively ending the Civil War. President Lincoln’s magnanimous terms—paroling Confederate soldiers and respecting their property—aimed to heal the nation rather than punish the vanquished. The historic meeting symbolized a "just and lasting peace," though the surrender was bittersweet, occurring just days after Lincoln's assassination.

Transgender visibility has reached a cultural tipping point in 2015, marked by President Obama's historic mention of the term in the State of the Union and Bruce Jenner's public transition to Caitlyn Jenner gracing the cover of Vanity Fair. This surge in media attention, including shows like "Transparent" and Laverne Cox's continued prominence, signals a significant shift in public discourse, with experts viewing it as a potential catalyst for civil rights progress. The national conversation now encompasses a broader spectrum of transgender experiences, from reality TV to academic theory, indicating that trans people

Jonty Hurwitz's microscopic sculpture "Trust," recognized as the smallest human form ever created, vanished while being photographed under an electron microscope, leaving only a smudged fingerprint. Despite an hour-long search by the artist and photographer, the "Nano-sculpture" was lost, though Hurwitz continues to create similarly tiny works using advanced two-photon lithography technology.

Around 117 migrants, mostly from sub-Saharan Africa, arrived in Augusta, Sicily after being rescued at sea off the coast of Libya, joining thousands of others who have made the dangerous journey this year. The group, which included 31 women and a pregnant woman, had endured harrowing conditions on unseaworthy vessels, with many fleeing war, poverty, and the threat of ISIS or Boko Haram. In "All-New X-Men" No. 40, Iceman (Bobby Drake) officially comes out as gay after fellow X-Men member Jean Grey confronts him about his past behavior. Writer Brian Michael Bendis revealed the storyline was intended to explore the personal journeys of mutants hiding their true selves, marking a significant moment for the long-running franchise. The reveal has sparked discussion about representation, coming as the character has been a staple of the X-Men since the team's inception.

The article argues that medical marijuana is experiencing a "revolution" in American society, marked by rapidly shifting public opinion and legislative changes. It highlights that support for legalization has surged, with 53% of Americans now in favor and 77% supporting medical use, driven by high-profile cases like children with epilepsy and even skeptical figures like the author's mother changing their views. The piece concludes that this shift represents a profound cultural turnaround, moving from stigma to widespread acceptance across diverse groups.

Fireball Cinnamon Whisky has rapidly become America's most popular party shot, surpassing established brands like Jim Beam and Jägermeister in retail sales. Its meteoric rise is attributed to its approachable sweetness and low alcohol content, making it especially appealing to young drinkers and women. However, the brand faces criticism from whiskey purists who consider it a "gateway" product that masks the taste of alcohol with cinnamon and sugar.

A 17-year-old mother was arrested for child abuse after her 4-month-old infant was hospitalized in critical condition; a day later, police discovered the body of her 3-year-old sister, who had been dead for weeks, leading to the mother's re-arrest on charges of abuse resulting in death. Sudan, the last known male northern white rhino, is under 24-hour armed guard at Kenya's Ol Pejeta Conservancy alongside two females, Fatu and Najin, as experts race to prevent the subspecies' extinction. While natural mating is complicated by Sudan's age and low sperm count, and Najin's physical limitations, scientists are exploring advanced techniques like in vitro fertilization and cross-breeding with southern white rhinos as a last-ditch effort to save the species.

The death toll from the Nepal earthquake has surpassed 3,000, with 3,218 confirmed dead in Nepal alone, as rescue efforts continue in the rugged countryside. International aid is focused on Kathmandu, where residents are enduring aftershocks, sleeping outdoors, and searching through rubble for survivors and missing family members.

Amnesty International is demanding an investigation into the police killings of 20 suspected red sandalwood smugglers in Andhra Pradesh, alleging the encounter was a "staged extrajudicial execution" since most victims were shot in the back. The group argues that lethal force was unjustified as no police were injured, and the National Human Rights Commission has labeled the incident a "serious violation of human rights." Local politicians have protested the killings, calling them "murder in cold blood," while police maintain the suspects attacked officers with axes and stones during a three-hour gun battle.

Jurors began deliberations Tuesday in the Boston Marathon bombing trial, where Dzhokhar Tsarnaev faces life in prison or the death penalty for his role in the attack. The prosecution argued Tsarnaev targeted civilians to "terrorize this country," while the defense focused on sparing his life. If found guilty of a capital count, the trial will move to a second phase to determine his sentence.

Boston prosecutors released body camera footage of the fatal shooting of Angelo West by Officer John Moynihan to address community concerns. The incident occurred in Roxbury when Moynihan opened West's car door, prompting West to fire first; Moynihan was wounded but survived, while West was killed at the scene. The release aimed to ensure transparency following the shooting, which sparked calls for calm from local leaders despite the officer's history of prior gun convictions.

Tulsa County Deputy Robert Bates faces a second-degree manslaughter charge after video shows him shouting "Taser" before fatally shooting Eric Harris with a handgun during an undercover sting. The incident has sparked outrage, with Harris' family demanding an independent investigation into what they call unjustified brutality, while Bates' attorney claims the shooting was an "excusable homicide" caused by confusion during the arrest.

Italian police reported that 12 Christian migrants were thrown overboard and killed by fellow Muslim passengers from the Ivory Coast, Mali, and Senegal during a voyage from Libya to Italy. Authorities have arrested 15 suspects and rescued the remaining passengers, who formed a human chain to prevent further killings. The incident highlights the extreme dangers and violence faced by migrants attempting the dangerous journey across the Mediterranean.

An Arizona police chief defended an officer's decision to drive into an armed suspect, stating that deadly force was justified despite the risk of death. The incident occurred when Mario Valencia, who had allegedly stolen a rifle and was involved in multiple crimes, was struck by a patrol car while walking in a business park. Valencia survived the impact and was subsequently charged, though his attorney argued the action constituted excessive force.

A 2-year-old boy was killed after being struck by a van at a birthday party in Milwaukee. The driver, Archie Brown Jr., was later shot and killed by Ricky Ricardo Chiles III, the uncle of the driver's son, Rasheed Chiles, who was also fatally shot while trying to help the toddler. The suspect died by suicide as police closed in, leaving two families devastated by a chain of retaliatory violence that began with a tragic accident.

A former New York police officer, Michael Rapiejko, intentionally drove his patrol car into an armed suspect, Mario Valencia, in Arizona after Valencia had fired a rifle in the air and pointed a gun at another officer. Rapiejko had previously faced a lawsuit in New York alleging he pointed a gun and choked a man during a 2005 arrest, which was settled for $20,000. Authorities justified the collision as necessary to prevent Valencia from harming others, noting that deadly force was authorized given the suspect's actions.

A migrant shipwreck off the coast of Italy may have killed hundreds, with authorities fearing three additional boats are in distress. European Union ministers have proposed a 10-point plan to increase search and rescue operations and combat human traffickers following a surge in Mediterranean crossings. The disaster highlights the deadly risks migrants face, with over 900 believed to have died crossing the sea this year alone.

Jim Clark determined that Tulsa County Reserve Deputy Robert Bates did not commit a crime when he shot Eric Harris, attributing the incident to "slip and capture," a phenomenon where an officer's trained response to deploy a Taser was overridden by a more well-rehearsed motor program to fire his handgun under extreme stress.
